    GPU acceleration¶

    Five estimators run part of their work on the GPU: UMAPGpu, DensMAPGpu, TSNEGpu, DREAMSGpu and PHATEGpu. The backend is wgpu, so there is no CUDA runtime to install, and the same wheel runs on Metal, Vulkan and DX12. This vignette covers what actually moves to the device, what it buys you, and the sharp edges.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

import manifolds_rs as mf

pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60)


def scatter(
    ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks."""
    ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])


def panels(
    embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10"
) -> None:
    """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False
    )
    for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True):
        scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap)
    fig.tight_layout()


def timed(fn) -> float:
    """Wall time of one call, in seconds."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    return time.perf_counter() - start
    import time import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import polars as pl import manifolds_rs as mf pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60) def scatter( ax: plt.Axes, emb: np.ndarray, c: np.ndarray, title: str, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """One embedding, coloured by `c`, without axis ticks.""" ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=c, s=1, cmap=cmap, alpha=0.6) ax.set_title(title) ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) def panels( embeddings: dict[str, np.ndarray], c: np.ndarray, cmap: str = "tab10" ) -> None: """A row of embeddings sharing one colouring.""" fig, axes = plt.subplots( 1, len(embeddings), figsize=(4.3 * len(embeddings), 4.3), squeeze=False ) for ax, (name, emb) in zip(axes[0], embeddings.items(), strict=True): scatter(ax, emb, c, name, cmap) fig.tight_layout() def timed(fn) -> float: """Wall time of one call, in seconds.""" start = time.perf_counter() fn() return time.perf_counter() - start

    One call answers both questions you have: was this build compiled with GPU support, and is there an adapter?

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    mf.gpu_available()
    mf.gpu_available()
    Out[2]:
    True

    What moves to the device¶

    Not everything.

    • UMAPGpu and DensMAPGpu: the neighbour search and the optimiser. "adam_gpu" (default) is the parallel Adam on the device, "adam_v06_gpu" the umap-learn 0.6 Adam. The CPU names still work and run the optimiser on the CPU after a GPU search. Graph construction and initialisation stay on the CPU. densMAP's density term runs on the device with "adam_gpu"; the radii come back to the host in between so the correlation statistics can accumulate in float64. The 0.6 Adam has no density term, so DensMAPGpu refuses both "adam_v06" names.
    • TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu: the neighbour search always. With approx="fft_3k_gpu" the whole optimisation stays on the device too: the three-kernel FFT repulsion, with the embedding resident between epochs. The other approx values run on the CPU after the GPU search.
    • PHATEGpu: the neighbour search and, with spectral landmarks, the randomised SVD and k-means of the landmark selection. Diffusion time, powering, MDS and interpolation stay on the CPU.

    Same data on both sides first, to see the pictures agree.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    X, y = mf.datasets.clustered(25_000)
X_traj, y_traj = mf.datasets.trajectory(25_000)
order = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(y_traj))

panels(
    {
        "UMAP": mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X),
        "UMAPGpu adam_gpu": mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X),
        "UMAPGpu adam_v06_gpu + recursive": mf.UMAPGpu(
            optimiser="adam_v06_gpu", init="recursive"
        ).fit_transform(X),
    },
    y,
)

    Same pictures on both sides. DREAMS sits apart because it is pulled towards its PCA reference, which is the point of it.

    Is it faster?¶

    That depends on whether the neighbour search and the optimiser were your bottleneck. On a few thousand points they won't be, and the transfers make the GPU slower than the CPU. Here are 200k points in 50 dimensions, one run each, wall time in seconds, neighbour search included.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    X_big, _ = mf.datasets.clustered(200_000)
X_big32 = X_big.astype(np.float32)

runs = {
    "UMAP": lambda: mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X_big32),
    "UMAPGpu": lambda: mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X_big32),
    "TSNE fft_3k": lambda: mf.TSNE(approx="fft_3k").fit_transform(X_big32),
    "TSNEGpu fft_3k_gpu": lambda: mf.TSNEGpu(approx="fft_3k_gpu").fit_transform(
        X_big32
    ),
    "PHATE": lambda: mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_big32),
    "PHATEGpu": lambda: mf.PHATEGpu().fit_transform(X_big32),
}
pl.DataFrame(
    [{"method": k, "seconds": timed(fn)} for k, fn in runs.items()]
).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))
    X_big, _ = mf.datasets.clustered(200_000) X_big32 = X_big.astype(np.float32) runs = { "UMAP": lambda: mf.UMAP().fit_transform(X_big32), "UMAPGpu": lambda: mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X_big32), "TSNE fft_3k": lambda: mf.TSNE(approx="fft_3k").fit_transform(X_big32), "TSNEGpu fft_3k_gpu": lambda: mf.TSNEGpu(approx="fft_3k_gpu").fit_transform( X_big32 ), "PHATE": lambda: mf.PHATE().fit_transform(X_big32), "PHATEGpu": lambda: mf.PHATEGpu().fit_transform(X_big32), } pl.DataFrame( [{"method": k, "seconds": timed(fn)} for k, fn in runs.items()] ).with_columns(pl.col("seconds").round(2))

    Both sides get float32 input, so the CPU side is not paying for float64. On the M1 Max these notebooks were executed on, the GPU is two and a half to three times faster for UMAP and t-SNE and about 1.5 times for PHATE, whose diffusion and MDS stay on the CPU. Measure on your own data and hardware before switching.

    Precision¶

    WGSL has no float64, so the GPU estimators run in float32 at any size. fit casts your input down, float64 included, and the embedding comes back as float32. That is the only silent narrowing of your input in the package. If it matters for your data, stay on the CPU estimators, which keep your dtype. PCA initialisation still runs in float64 on the CPU and is cast back.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X[:2_000]).dtype
    mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X[:2_000]).dtype
    Out[7]:
    dtype('float32')

    Reproducibility¶

    GPU embeddings are reproducible in structure, not always in coordinates. The device neighbour searches are not bit-stable at scale, and 500 epochs of Adam turn a tiny difference in the graph into visibly different coordinates. The clusters, branches and separations come back; the exact positions may not. The Adam update itself is bit-stable given a fixed graph, so hand in a pre-computed graph and a GPU run is reproducible too.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X, k=15, ann="nndescent")
{
    "same graph, run twice": np.array_equal(
        mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist),
        mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist),
    )
}
    idx, dist = mf.knn_graph(X, k=15, ann="nndescent") { "same graph, run twice": np.array_equal( mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist), mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist), ) }
    Out[8]:
    {'same graph, run twice': True}

    PHATE picks its diffusion time from the graph, so a different backend can pick a different t. Pin t when you compare runs.

    Neighbour backends¶

    The device backends are not the CPU ones with a suffix. "nndescent_gpu" runs NN-Descent on the device and is the default for UMAPGpu, DensMAPGpu and PHATEGpu. TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu ask for 3 * perplexity neighbours and default to "ivf_gpu", which holds up better at that k. "exhaustive_gpu" is the third. A CPU-only name like "hnsw" is an error, not a silent fallback. The knobs live in NeighbourParamsGpu, a different set from the CPU NeighbourParams.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    mf.NeighbourParamsGpu()
    mf.NeighbourParamsGpu()
    Out[9]:
    NeighbourParamsGpu(n_list=None, n_probes=None, k_means=None, k_build=None, n_tree=None, delta=None, rho=None)

    Mixing CPU and GPU¶

    The neighbour graph is two arrays, so build it wherever it is cheapest and hand it to whichever estimator you like. The graph above came from the CPU; here it feeds the GPU optimiser, and the GPU search is skipped entirely.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    panels(
    {
        "CPU graph, GPU Adam": mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform(
            X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist
        )
    },
    y,
)
    panels( { "CPU graph, GPU Adam": mf.UMAPGpu().fit_transform( X, knn_indices=idx, knn_distances=dist ) }, y, )

    Headless machines and CI¶

    gpu_available() returns False on a box with no adapter rather than raising, and the GPU estimators still import. That is deliberate: a hosted CI runner can prove the GPU wheel builds and degrades cleanly without a device. It cannot prove the kernels are correct. That needs a runner with a GPU.

    MLX on Apple Silicon¶

    There is a second Apple GPU path, through MLX via mlx-c, and it is not in the published wheel. It links mlx-c dynamically, so a wheel carrying it fails to import on any Mac without the library. Build it yourself:

    brew install mlx-c
maturin develop --release --features mlx

    mf.mlx_available() is True only in an mlx build that found mlx-c. MLX is not a separate set of estimators; the CPU estimators gain a few extra names:

    mf.UMAP(ann="nndescent_mlx", optimiser="adam_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.DensMAP(optimiser="adam_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.TSNE(ann="nndescent_mlx", approx="fft_3k_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.DREAMS(approx="fft_3k_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.PHATE(ann="nndescent_mlx", landmark_method="spectral_mlx").fit_transform(X)
mf.knn_graph(X, k=15, ann="ivf_mlx")

    The neighbour backends are "exhaustive_mlx", "ivf_mlx" and "nndescent_mlx". TSNEGpu and DREAMSGpu take approx="fft_3k_mlx" as well, with the search on wgpu and the optimiser on MLX. PHATEGpu takes landmark_method="spectral_mlx" the same way. den-SNE has no MLX path, and DiffusionMaps keeps its landmark selection on the CPU. Everything MLX runs in float32. In a build without MLX these names are refused with a pointer to the build flag.

    Is it worth the trouble? See the wgpu vs MLX benchmarks.
